title: How Icebergs Work (Very Cool)
summary: Josh and Chuck explore icebergs: how they form from calving glaciers and ice shelves (mostly Greenland and Antarctica), why they float (freshwater ice is less dense than seawater, with roughly one-sixth to one-ninth showing above water), their color and roll-over risks, life cycle and drift driven by currents rather than wind, and their ecological role in nutrient release and carbon sequestration. They cover famous iceberg sinkings (the Titanic, Lady of the Lake, Hans Hedtoft), iceberg size classifications (growler, bergy bit, small, medium, large, very large) and shapes (tabular, non-tabular), the B-15 iceberg, proposals to tow icebergs for drinking water, the International Ice Patrol and Iceberg Alley, and a tangent on the nautical mile. The episode closes with a horror fiction contest announcement and a listener mail segment about language evolution and vervet monkey calls.

entities.name: Grooming, Gossip and the Evolution of Language

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat casually about their week and computers before turning to the topic of icebergs and the sinking of the William Carson.

segments.title: Famous iceberg sinkings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the William Carson sinking off Labrador in 1913 with no lives lost but cars lost, then the Lady of the Lake, and the Hans Hedtoft off Greenland on its maiden voyage in 1959 with all aboard lost. They note many passenger liners were lost in Iceberg Alley between 1882 and 1914.

segments.title: Glaciers and how icebergs form
segments.summary: Glaciers are described as accumulated compressed snow that flows downhill, becoming dense blue ice. Glacier pieces break off by calving at the edge of ice shelves, and freshwater icebergs float into the sea. Major ice shelves are on Greenland's western coast and ringing Antarctica.

segments.title: Why ice floats and the tip of the iceberg
segments.summary: Freshwater freezes at 32 F and seawater at a lower temperature. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats, and about one-sixth to one-ninth of an iceberg shows above water. Variation in seawater salinity and iceberg density changes the visible proportion.

segments.title: Iceberg color, rolling, and thermal shock
segments.summary: Glacial ice is blue, while trapped air can make icebergs white and old ice under Antarctic shelves can look green. Icebergs can roll over without warning, as in a New Zealand helicopter tour incident. Melting ice can crack and shatter from thermal shock, as described by Gregory Stone's account of an iceberg breaking apart.

segments.title: Iceberg life cycle, drift, and size classes
segments.summary: Icebergs may last years, with northern ones drifting for decades and southern ones melting faster in warmer water, sometimes reaching Bermuda. Icebergs are moved by currents rather than wind, and they can scrape the seafloor. Size classes run from growler and bergy bit to small, medium, large, and very large, and shapes are tabular or non-tabular. The B-15 iceberg from the Ross ice shelf was about the size of Jamaica.

segments.title: Iceberg ecology, carbon, and drinking water
segments.summary: Melting icebergs release fresh water and iron-rich nutrients that support algae, krill, fish, and birds, and they help sequester carbon in the ocean. Icebergs can disrupt shipping and affect Emperor Penguins, as in March of the Penguins. A RAND Corporation study looked at towing icebergs for drinking water, with cost estimates, and an MIT pipeline proposal from Alaska was considered too expensive.

segments.title: International Ice Patrol and iceberg monitoring
segments.summary: The International Ice Patrol, administered by the US Coast Guard, tracks icebergs and warns ships, marking a limit of all known ice. The Coast Guard has also spray painted icebergs and attached radio transmitters to them.

segments.title: Nautical mile tangent
segments.summary: Josh explains that a nautical mile is about 1.158 statute miles because it accounts for the curvature of the Earth, and that the French Academy of Sciences defined the kilometer based on the distance from the North Pole to the equator through Paris.

segments.title: Horror fiction contest announcement
segments.summary: The hosts announce a listener horror fiction contest with 3,000 to 4,000 word submissions judged on criteria, with the top 16 put to a listener vote and read as the Halloween episode.

segments.title: Listener mail on language and vervet monkeys
segments.summary: A listener from Chicago, Matt Schunk, describes Robin Dunbar's book Grooming, Gossip and the Evolution of Language and a study of vervet monkey alarm calls. The hosts sign off with a request for book recommendations.
